lesson.title: Fat Tails and Fair Warnings: T Versus Z
lesson.summary: The t-distribution and the standard normal (z) distribution share the same basic shape, but the t-distribution's heavier tails mean more extreme values are treated as plausible, especially with small samples.
lesson.body:
Placed side by side, a t-distribution and the standard normal curve look almost like the same shape at first glance: both are symmetric, unimodal, bell-shaped, and centered at 0. The difference is in the tails. The t-distribution assigns more probability to values far from 0 than the standard normal curve does, which is why it is described as having heavier tails. This is not a minor cosmetic difference, it directly affects how extreme a test statistic has to be before it counts as convincing evidence, and how wide a confidence interval needs to be to reach a given confidence level.

The reason traces directly back to where each distribution comes from. The standard normal distribution describes a statistic built using the true, known population standard deviation, sigma. There is exactly one source of randomness in that statistic: the sample mean bouncing around from sample to sample. The t-distribution describes a statistic built using s, the estimated standard deviation, in place of sigma, which adds a second source of randomness, since s itself bounces around from sample to sample, sometimes coming in smaller than sigma and sometimes larger. That second source of variability is what fattens the tails of the t-distribution relative to z.

This gap between t and z is not fixed, it shrinks as degrees of freedom increases. With a small sample, say df = 5, the t-distribution's tails are noticeably heavier than the normal curve's. With a large sample, say df = 100, the t-distribution is nearly indistinguishable from the standard normal curve, because s has become a precise enough estimate of sigma that the extra uncertainty is negligible. The practical consequence is that whenever sigma is unknown, which is nearly always in real research, t-procedures should be used instead of z-procedures, and this matters most, and looks most different from a z result, precisely when sample sizes are small. The next section turns this qualitative difference into exact numbers, by comparing t and z critical values directly.
